By one who is ignorant of what is a field and what is not a field, and who merely follows what has been heard.

Whatever words unworthy of praise were previously spoken by me out of dullness— having failed to distinguish between what is a field of merit and what is not, and having merely followed after sounds— [I confess them].
Whatever praise I previously uttered for what is blameworthy— out of ignorance regarding what constitutes a "field" and what does not, and merely following tradition— I have erred.

O Sage, this washing away of the mud-stain of my speech is undertaken by me, beginning with you, who are a moving holy pilgrimage site. (2) The washing away of that which is stained by the mud of speech—this is undertaken by me, O Sage, with respect to you, a moving holy pilgrimage site. (2)
Relying upon you who have departed [into nirvāṇa], I compose this work as a purificatory bath for that defilement of the mud of speech, O Silent One, you who are a moving place of pilgrimage.
Whatever offense I have committed against the masses of excellent ones out of delusion or blindness, [may it be forgiven].
May this *aghamaṛṣaṇa*, the purifier, be for me the cleansing of that evil.
Whatever offense I have committed against the supreme assembly through the blindness of delusion— may this be the purifier that removes the stain of that sin.
Furthermore, whatever I have failed to do out of the blindness of my ignorance toward the assembly of the Noble Ones—may this work serve as a purifying rite to cleanse that evil deed of mine!
May my two types of vocal action remain inseparable from cessation until the very end:
that which consists of your own words and that which takes refuge in your virtues. (4)
Until my parinirvāṇa, may I not be deprived of these two kinds of speech: your own words and those that take their support from your qualities.
If I were to say this very thing, there would be a fragmentation of my speech;
for this alone is the essence of discourse, and anything other than this is merely the cawing of a crow. (5) Since this much alone is the core of the matter, there is no purpose in anything else.
"Let me speak only this, or else let me remain silent.
Let me speak only so long as there is no interruption of my speech; for in that regard alone is speech essential—anything other than this is merely the cawing of a crow.
Your very nature is what provides you with equality, and it is from you alone that it is obtained.
But all other phenomena do not enter into your presence.
Your dharma alone is yours; you possess it as being equal to yourself. Therefore, all other phenomena are not superior to you.

Only through your Dharma and only through you can equality with you be found; all other dharmas, however, do not approach your presence. If the qualities of a Buddha are brought before one's eyes, everything else is surpassed; the remainder becomes like mere refuse. (7)
If one contemplates the qualities of the Buddha,
they become supreme above all things; every other entity, by contrast, becomes like impurity itself.
There is no one at all who is your equal; what path of speech could there be for one superior?
Not even anyone slightly inferior or separated by a small degree exists for you.
(8) Since there is not even one person like you, what need is there to mention one who is superior?
There is no one even slightly inferior to you in any respect; what possibility is there of speaking of one who is superior? Not even one who is but a little less than you can be found.
O Leader, you are one who cannot be led; whom then shall I lead to you?
Homage be to you, the peerless one, for whom there is no room for comparison; O Guide,
since no example can be found to describe you,
homage to you who have eliminated the very possibility of analogy!
By what means, then, could I bring you here? You are not to be brought here, O Leader; homage to you, the incomparable one, for whom no analogy can be found!
Even with other individuals who have attained the commonality of liberation, there is a vast difference between them and you because of your incomparable Buddha-qualities. (10)
Because the Buddha-qualities are immeasurable, even those other persons who have attained a liberation similar to yours differ from you by a vast margin.

For who, being ignorant of distinctions, would reflect space through the tiny opening of a pore of the skin merely because of the commonality of its emptiness? (11) Because they are similar in being empty, who, failing to perceive their distinction, [would act thus]?

Who indeed, lacking discernment, would compare the empty pore of a single hair to the vastness of space on the basis of their mere emptiness? Who could count the incalculable, and who could measure the immeasurable?

Indeed, no determination exists among your qualities by way of number or power: Who can count that which is numberless? Who can measure that which is immeasurable? There is no means of estimating the number or the power of your virtues.
Who could count those who are beyond counting, or measure those who are immeasurable? For there is no limit to your qualities in terms of their number or power.
I find no satisfaction, nor do I reach the end of your virtuous conduct, like one wandering through a boundless forest of wish-fulfilling trees. 13
Just as one might wander within a vast grove of wish-fulfilling trees, I find neither satiety nor an end to your excellent conduct, as if roaming through an infinite forest of kalpavṛkṣas.
O Ocean of Qualities, if these qualities of a Tathāgata were visible, there would be no room for them even in space. (14)
If these dharmas of the Tathāgata were demonstrable, there would be no space even in the sky for them, O Ocean of Qualities! [This was said] by your Dharma General, the banner of all Śrāvakas.

By way of praising his unsurpassedness, [the Buddha said]: "To you who stands in your very presence, the leader of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the crest-jewel of all śrāvakas, who proclaims the profound [Dharma]— [The verse continues: Having directly attended upon you, The leader of the Dharma of the Buddhas, The crest-jewel of all śrāvakas, Who proclaims the profound [Dharma], I shall now speak of the qualities Of that son of the Sugata.

By your commander-in-chief of the Dharma, who is the banner of all listeners, and by him who serves you in person with the explanation of the unsurpassed [teachings], it has been explained by one who is devoted regarding the knowledge of the Buddha’s Dharma.
By saying "no," the Blessed One [revealed] the inexhaustible profundity of the Buddha-dharma. Because he was omniscient, when questioned by the Blessed One, he replied, "I do not know."

The profound nature of the Buddha-dharma was explained by him without having fully realized it; thus, when questioned regarding his knowledge of the Buddha-dharmas, he declared that the imperishable profundity of the Buddha-dharmas is "not so."

I shall honor you with virtues extracted from your very teaching, just as one honors a jewel mine with its own gems, a mountain with its own minerals, a sandalwood tree with its own fragrance, or a lake with its own lotuses.
Just as a gold-extracting gem is honored by the very gold produced from its own melting,
so too are you honored by those very qualities that have been extracted solely from your own teaching.

I shall praise you with qualities drawn from your own teaching, just as a jewel that spews gold is praised with gold extracted from itself. The moonlight, though spreading everywhere from the vault of the sky, does not reach its full utility; nor does [the light of] a lamp [attain such]... (25)
The moonlight does not stream forth and descend in its entirety from the center of the sky;
yet, when the moonlight falls upon the earth and the buds open, the groves of *kumuda* lilies do not fail to bloom.
Indeed, not all of the moonlight that penetrates everywhere from the firmament is put to use; yet, there is no field of *kumuda* lotuses that does not bloom when [the light] descends upon the earth.
And so it is with you: although the shore of the ocean of praises for the Lord of Munis is immeasurable, there is no person who is not joined with their desired fruit. (26)

Likewise, for those endowed with faith who express even a single portion of the infinite ocean of the Victorious One’s praises— which possesses immeasurable waters of excellent qualities— they shall not fail to obtain the fruit of their desires.

Likewise, there is no other shore to the ocean of praises for the Silent Sage among kings, whose waters are your immeasurable qualities; yet, if one enumerates even a portion of them with faith, that person does not remain without the desired fruit.
His birth is fruitful, his life is free from calamity, his path is beyond duality, and his state is like that of the sun.

And from this [verse] follows the praise of the Buddha’s qualities, beginning with faith and so forth: The words that proclaim the praises of the Buddha are fruitful; they are a profitable cargo for rebirth, a path of ease free from obstacles, and the root of qualities such as faith, which leads to the vehicle of Brahmā. From these and other [qualities], there arises the golden dust [of virtue]. (27)

Fertility [of speech], the precious essence of birth, the unobstructed and auspicious path, the pure vehicle, and the accumulation of qualities such as faith and so forth—therefore, this is the recitation of the praise of the Buddha:

"For those engaged in composing this hymn to the Buddha, when their faculties are bowed down by devotion and melting with love, no one who is not omniscient is able to measure the surge of Dharma that occurs in each and every moment. (28)
Those whose faculties are fully inclined toward faith and who strive in the compositions that praise the Buddha—
whatever stream of Dharma arises for them in every single moment cannot be grasped even in part by one who is not omniscient.

No one who is not omniscient is capable of measuring the agitation that arises in every single moment for those engaged in composing a praise of the Buddha, while their senses—bent forward by devotion—rush toward it;
for even when there is the power of such activity, it is characterized by restlessness, and because this attainment of union is exceedingly marvelous.
For those who do not apply themselves to this practice, what deception could be greater than that?
(29) Since the possession of power is impermanent and this leisure and opportunity is extremely difficult to find, what greater deception could there be for those who do not strive in this action?

When the faculties are present and skill is not yet fixed, and because this auspicious constellation is so exceedingly wonderful, what other self-deception could there be for those who do not direct their efforts toward that task?

The First Chapter: "Praising the Ineffable" from the *Praise of the Worthy of Praise*, a hymn to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Just as I was beheld by you, O Buddha, with your awakened eye moistened by compassion, while I stood with my senses inclined toward devotion to you.
While you, Blessed One, remain present, I have become one who is inclined toward the power of faith;
for what reason do you gaze upon me with the Buddha-eye, moistened by compassion?

Just as I am perceived by you with that compassionate Buddha-eye resting upon me—one whose senses are directed toward devotion to you—O Buddha, I now bring that very same compassion of yours, directed toward myself, into immediate presence;
I act as if it were manifest before my eyes. Homage to the Worthy One! Homage be to you! 2.
Bringing to mind that very compassion of yours directed toward me, I prostrate to you, who are worthy of worship, as if you were present before my eyes.
Who, not being omniscient, could ever understand you, the Omniscient One? Homage be to you, whose vast majesty is known only by yourself!
Who, not being all-knowing, could ever understand you, the All-Knowing One? How could they comprehend you? Homage be to you, whose extensive greatness is self-evident!
Homage to you, the Omniscient One, whose own greatness is vast and who knows it yourself!
How could one who is not omniscient comprehend you, the Omniscient One? For one such as I, there is no way to understand that "you were exactly like this."
Whoever you are and however you are—homage be to you as such!
"You are this" or "you are like that"—you are not an object for one such as I.
Since I do not know who you are or what you are like, I pay homage to you as you truly are.
“You are such and of such a nature”—this is not a path for one like me; whoever you are and whatever your qualities may be, homage be to you who are thus endowed!
“O Protector, as you yourself are, and as are the Victors like you—[whatever their nature may be], homage be to you who are thus endowed! (5)
O Protector, you are just like yourself; as are the Victors who resemble you, so is there no other whatsoever who is like you. To you, who are thus, I prostrate.
Just as you yourself know yourself, and just as those like you know you— [just as those like me know you]—
homage be to you, who are such!
(6) Just as you yourself know, and just as those like you know you...
Homage to you who, such as you are, are not known by others, but are known by yourself through your own qualities, such as the ten powers, and likewise by those who are equal to you.
Revealed through compassion— to you who are such, let there be homage!
(7) Just as you yourself have made manifest through compassion the qualities such as the ten powers, to you who are such, I prostrate.

Just as you yourself have manifested the self through qualities such as the ten powers out of compassion, homage be to you who are thus constituted! Therefore, having extracted the very essence from the mine of your virtues, we shall act according to our ability; henceforth, let there be homage to you! (8)
From this day forward, having extracted the very essence from that mine of your qualities, I shall act according to my ability; to you, I pay homage.
Homage to the Arhat! Homage be to you; homage be to you, to the Arhat!
Homage, homage, let there be homage to you; homage be to you, homage to the Arhat! (9) I prostrate and bow before you, O Arhat; I prostrate and bow before you, O Worthy One.

Homage to you, O Reasoning One; I bow to you, I pay homage to you. Homage to the Arhat; homage be to you, homage be to you, the one worthy of homage. Homage, homage, homage be to you; homage be to you, homage to you, O Worthy One! *namaḥ saṃbuddharatnāya* [homage to the Jewel of the Perfectly Awakened One]. *dharmaratna...* [Jewel of the Dharma...]
Homage to you, the mine of the Jewel of the Saṅgha, the assembly of the Three Jewels!
You are the Perfect Buddha, the Jewel; you are the nature of the Jewel of the Dharma;
you are the source of the Jewel of the Saṅgha. I bow to you, the gathering of the Three Jewels.

Homage to you, the Jewel of the Fully Awakened One, who possesses the Jewel of the Dharma as your very nature, who is the mine of the Jewel of the Saṃgha, and who embodies the Three Jewels within yourself!
Homage to you, whose self-nature is the jewel of form, whose inner self is the jewel of mind, who is the source of the jewel of Dharma, and who is the embodiment of all jewels! (11)
Worthy of worship, you are a jewel; your enlightened intent is also a jewel.
You are the source of the precious sublime Dharma; to you, the universal jewel, I prostrate!

In this verse, he who possesses the jewel of the form-body as the realization of his own physical being, and the jewel of the mind as his inner self, and who is the mine of the jewel of the Dharma—to that Universal Jewel, homage!
Homage to you, who have become the supreme among all jewels, who outshine all jewels, who are the source of all jewels,
and who are the true jewel.
(12) Because you have become the most excellent of all jewels, you outshine all jewels.
Homage to you, the source of all jewels; homage to you, the true jewel, who surpasses all jewels and is the treasury of every gem.
*namas te rūparatnāya cittaratnāya te namaḥ* (Homage to you, the jewel of form; homage to you, the jewel of mind).
Homage to you, the jewel of the Dharma; homage to you, the jewel of all things.
I prostrate to you, whose mind is a jewel;
I prostrate to you, the Dharma that is a jewel; I prostrate to the jewel of all.

Homage to you whose form is a jewel; homage to you whose mind is a jewel; homage to you whose Dharma is a jewel; homage to you, the Universal Jewel! Homage to you, the Unconditioned, to the Worthy One worthy of homage, to the Arhat—may there be devotion to you, whose self is cultivated through the meditation on the existence and non-existence of becoming. (14)

To you, the Arhat worthy of homage, who has become the supreme among all Sages through mastery in meditating upon the non-existence of phenomenal existence— to you, the Unbending One, I pay respectful salutation.
Homage be to you, who are untransgressable, who abide at the limit of perfection,
and who are the unsurpassed boundary of the ascetic life! (15) To you who are impossible to overstep, And who dwell in the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), [homage be to you].
Homage to you, the unsurpassed one who has reached the ultimate goal of the ascetic life,
the inviolable one who abides at the limit of perfection, the supreme one who defines the bounds of the *śramaṇa*. To you who are endowed with every excellence and who surpass all splendor, [homage].
Homage to you, the Buddha-lotus, who is delightful in all seasons, who outshines all other beauties through the perfection of every aspect, and who brings joy at all times.
(16) I bow to you, the Buddha-lotus, who, through the excellence of all aspects, eclipses all other splendors and gladdens beings in every season. (16)
Homage to you, who possess all forms, who surpasses all beauties, who is charming in every season, the blossomed lotus—homage to you!
Homage to the golden one, the fragrant one, the beautiful one, the awakened white lotus, the blossomed and unfading one. (17)
To you, the well-colored, sweet-smelling, beautiful to behold, and unfading— the fully awakened Buddha who is like a white lotus in full bloom— I pay homage.
Homage to you, the delicate ascetic, who has attained at will the contact with the essence of the bliss of pliancy.
Homage to you, the most youthful among ascetics, who dwell in bliss and have attained the ultimate perfection of the entire fruit of asceticism. śramaṇaphalasākalyam anuprāptāya naiṣṭhikam |
Homage be to you, the ascetic who has pledged to speak the truth;
having reached the ultimate goal through the attainment of the fruit of enlightenment,
you are the Śramaṇa who has vowed to proclaim the sublime Dharma.

Homage be to you, the Brahmin, who has attained the entire and supreme fruit of your exertion, who has realized the true designation, and who is purified by knowledge and conduct; homage be to you, the ascetic! The noble Dharma is unassailable,
and the noble activity is sublime; acting as the teacher of the world— to you, O Noble One, I prostrate.
To him whose noble *dharma* is unshakable, whose noble conduct is to be taken as the standard, to the Noble One who has performed what was to be done, to the Teacher of the World— to you, homage!
To him whose mind has been purified by the undertaking of asceticism and vows...
Homage be to you, the accomplished one who has bathed away all evils; To you, the *snātaka*, whose mind is made pure by having correctly undertaken ascetic vows and observances,
and who has washed away every sin— to you, the performer of ritual ablution, I prostrate.
Homage be to you, who have purified your mind by undertaking the ascetic vows, who have washed away all transgressions, and who have performed the ritual bath!
Homage be to you, the Lion among Men, who has attained supreme sovereignty, who overcomes all sentient beings, and whose lion’s roar resounds everywhere! (23)
Homage to you,
O Lion, who has attained supreme sovereignty, who outshines all sentient beings, and who lets forth the roar of a lion!
Homage to you, the Great Naga, who possesses the great footprint of the Avadāna, who relies upon the lofty mountain of the True Dharma,
and who has mastered all the dharmas that are to be known. (24) Homage to you, the Great Naga, who dwells upon the high peak of the Sublime Dharma and has realized the great path of the Avadānas.

Homage to you, Great Elephant, the destroyer of all other phenomena, whose deeds are recounted in grand narratives, who frequents the heights of the true Dharma, and who shatters all things. [You possess] a dignity superior to that of the Dharma, which cannot be withstood by anyone other than you.
Homage to you, who have gone forth having taken up the burden, the leader of the world.

Homage to you, the path for the world, who have traveled along the way of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)—a path that is extremely difficult and which no one other than you could endure. I prostrate to you.
Homage to you, the world’s beast of burden, who have set out after taking up the yoke that is uniquely yours to bear and is by its very nature exceedingly heavy;

To you who are exceedingly gentle, well-tamed, and patient; who possess speed, a beautiful complexion, and strength;

To the Gentle One, the Well-Tamed, the Patient, the one of perfected form, endowed with swiftness, beauty, and power, of noble lineage—to you, I pay homage.
Homage to you, who know the directions, the sacred fords, and the spheres of activity;
who are steadfast, whose gait is straight, and who have attained the preeminent state of the Bull.
(27) Omniscient in the directions, the sacred fords, and the spheres of conduct; firm, with a straight course and no crookedness.

Homage to you, O Bull, who has attained the station of the preeminent leader; who knows the directions, bathing places, and pastures; who is steadfast and walks upon the straight path; to you, the Bull who has achieved the status of the Great Leader.
To him who is skilled in the completeness of the means for taming, and who is free from weariness.
Homage to you, the supreme charioteer of those men who are to be tamed! (28) To you,
the supreme charioteer of those men to be tamed— skilled in every means of training and free from indolence— I pay homage.
Homage to you, who are skilled in the entirety of the means for subduing [beings], who are untiring, the most excellent charioteer of those humans who are to be disciplined!
Even one who is capable [of success] finds no other way than through your teaching;
therefore, homage to you, who are the embodiment of the complete holy life (*brahmacarya*). (29)
Since even a fortunate person would be without purpose outside of your teaching, I pay homage to you, who have become the embodiment of the complete pure conduct for all.

Homage, homage to you, the Great One, the Peerless One, the Ascetic; homage, homage to the Worthy One, the Greatly Worthy, the Arhat.

Homage be to you, whose awakening is stainless and fully blossomed; homage be to you, whose self is cultivated by a multitude of virtues.
Homage to you who possess a peerless and delightful body; homage to you who loudly proclaim the most sublime and melodious speech;

Homage to you who possess a form of incomparable beauty! Homage to you who speak with honeyed sweetness! Homage to you who possess stainless, awakened insight! Homage to you whose nature is unfolded by the multitude of qualities!

Neither omniscience, nor ascetic vows, nor all sacred fords, nor auspicious rites can touch even a fraction of the homage paid to the Buddha, which is rendered pure by the cultivation of the state of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). (72)
By thinking "the field," one bows to the Buddha; neither all stainless auspiciousness, nor all sacrifices, nor asceticism and vows, nor any ritual ablutions can equal it.

Neither all sacrifices nor ascetic practices, neither all places of pilgrimage nor auspicious mantras can equal even a sixteenth part of a prostration to the Buddha that is stainless because it is prompted by the discernment of the [true] field of merit. It spreads fame, upholds excellence, increases splendor, destroys all evil, and dispels every hostility.

The salutation to the Lord of Munis makes the lineage of men in this world certain of a happy rebirth; it bears fruit for their ultimate welfare and necessarily uproots all evils while increasing one’s splendor. (73) Saluting the Lord of Munis brings renown and glory; it eradicates all sins and causes majesty to flourish.
It dispels all enemies; it ensures that the continuum of people in the world is certain to reach a happy rebirth, and it ripens into the fruit of peace in the ultimate end.

It spreads renown, it bestows happiness, it causes splendor to increase, and it causes all evil to wane; it eliminates every enmity and creates a mental disposition firmly bound to an auspicious rebirth within the world of humans; and at the end, the practice of honoring the King of Sages surely ripens into peace.

All phenomena of all times are, for you, mines of every aspect.

All phenomena (*dharmas*), which can be known at all times and are the source of all appearances, come within the range of your insight like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of your hand, O Buddha.
Whether phenomena are distinct or identical, whether they are conditioned or unconditioned, your intellect is never obstructed, just as the movement of the wind is unimpeded in the sky. (11)
Whether phenomena are mobile or immobile, whether they are one or manifold, your mind encounters no obstruction, just as the wind moves through the sky.
In that way, you have thoroughly penetrated the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) such that, through the mere generation of a thought, everything is accomplished at your will. 12.
By performing your activities, you [act] such that through the mere generation of a thought...
For you, everything is accomplished according to your will; thus have you well penetrated the dharmadhātu.
O you who have reached the limit of virtue, there is no longer for you any wholesome deed that requires effort.
Your power to resolve at will is bound to mere intention.
For you who have reached the ultimate limit of virtue, there is no virtue that arises from effort; whatever you desire depends solely upon your mere wish.

For you, who abide in the goal of the wholesome, there is no longer any wholesome state associated with effort; for you, the supernormal power of choosing your own place of residence depends solely upon your wish.

The true existence of phenomena (*dharmasadbhāva*), their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), and their functional capacity (*dharmaśakti*) exist individually, established together with their causes and conditions, and accompanied by their results. (14)
The true nature of phenomena, their fundamental law, and the powers of phenomena— each existing with its primary cause and its arrangement, together with its secondary conditions and its fruits.

O Knower of all phenomena, you alone—and no other—comprehend in every way all those [beings], who possess various elements and distinctions, along with their full extent of arising, perishing, and the means for their decline and progress.

O Omniscient One, you understand everything in every way, and no one else;

Though hidden by a mountain, it is revealed to you; though very far away, it is near to you.

Even that which is deeply hidden is manifest to you; even that which is very distant is near; even that which is extremely turbid is instantly purified; and even that which is exceedingly high is low. (16)

Even that which is well-concealed is manifest to you; even that which is far distant is near to you; even that which is profoundly deep is inclined toward you; even that which is exceedingly high is minute for you. Even the pitch-black darkness is illuminated by you; even that which is divided by great doubt is certain to you; even the object of knowledge that is most profound is, for you, as utterly plain as the surface of the earth. (17)
Even the profound darkness appears as light; even that which is utterly uncertain is certain; even the most profound object of knowledge lies clearly open before you.
Even though the nature of phenomena is most profound, it does not produce weariness in you,

(18) Just like the golden waist-belt of the great Indra’s elephant.
Although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is exceedingly profound, you do not become weary or faint; just as the golden elephant-girth does not cause exhaustion to the elephant of Great Indra,

You are the foremost of all sentient beings, just as Buddhahood is among all perfections.

As liberation is among purities, as emptiness is among the principles (tattvas),

Whatever occurred in beginningless existence and whatever will occur in the endless future—[you know it all].
Your vision of knowledge operates there as if it were direct perception:
regarding that which arose in beginningless existence and that which will arise without end,
your wisdom engages in seeing them as if they were manifest before you.

O Sovereign, you are indeed the All-Knowing and the All-Conquering; it is none other than you.

That is merely a skillful means of discipline; it is not [done] out of power.
[It is] that which causes one who possesses false pride to be free from arrogance. 18.
That which causes some who possess false pride to be free from haughtiness.

Regarding what is said in the world, "Everything is conquered by the powerful," [this is merely a means for training].

“Everything is conquered by the powerful,” as it is said in the world; this is beyond dispute [even for others, but in you, O Leader, this state is perfected]. You are one who cannot be incited [to anger], you are blameless, and you have attained security. (20)
O Guide, no one is able to challenge you in accordance with the Dharma; you are beyond reproach, faultless, and have attained the state of bliss.
And he who delights in [the Dharma], being free from transgression, need not guard the four from anything; for when these four are complete, one should rely upon them.

Having crossed the entire ocean of the knowable, having abandoned all habitual tendencies forever, knowing the specific characteristics of all obstacles, and being skilled in all paths leading to definitive deliverance.

that and that is called an obscuration; that and that is an inexhaustible obscuration.

All phenomena are selfless; all conditioned things are momentary;
that which is called "nirvāṇa" is peace—these three characteristics are the seal of the Dharma.

"All dharmas are without self; all that is conditioned is momentary; nirvāṇa is peace"—having established this seal of the Dharma, which possesses these three characteristics, you have rendered all doctrines indestructible. For who, having spoken thus, could ever transcend the true nature of the world? 2
You have established that which is not the domain of any discourse and is indivisible; for who in this world, no matter what they might say, can ever transcend intrinsic nature?

Who, even by means of repeated practice in debate, is able to make that which is established otherwise, just as one cannot make coldness into heat? (3) Even though one has practiced the incantations of the *gal 'dzin pa*, who [could do so]?
Who could,
in a debate, overturn the truth by means of an argument rendered irresistible through oaths, as if one could turn heat into cold?
Even if someone were to inflict a wound upon the non-resistant sky...
But in this Dharma-seal, there is nothing whatsoever that contradicts the Dharma.
Just as it is possible for someone to wound the unobstructed sky,
so too there is no contradiction with the Dharma regarding this Dharma-seal.
Even if someone were to inflict an injury upon the sky, which offers no resistance, no one could do so to this seal of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
This is well known as the illustration of the two extremes of black and white;
it belongs only to your teaching, O Knower of the Reality of Dharma, and not to that of any other proponent. (5)

O Knower of the very nature of phenomena, it is through the teaching of your commands— the *Mahākāla* and the *Mahānīla*— that this [reality] is renowned; it does not exist in the teachings of any other speaker.
While the world has fallen into dispute by relying on various views,
you alone have awakened to the state that is free from dispute. Because they rely on diverse views, the worlds fall into contention.

While the entire world lies in dispute because each adheres to its own particular view, you alone have realized the state that is free from contention. Just as one with sight perceives forms while the blind are quarreling, you alone have understood the ground of non-dispute.
Just as one does not enter into dispute with those who are blind when they argue about forms seen by those with eyes— that very thing is your analogy for the foolish.
Just as one who sees forms does not engage in dispute while the blind are quarreling, so is this the analogy for you in relation to fools:
there is no dispute with anyone regarding your speech on the Dharma;
because you speak what is true, you do not dispute with the wise, nor with the ignorant, due to their lack of respect.
For you who speak according to the Dharma, there is no dispute with anyone whatsoever: not with the wise, because they speak well; nor with the unwise, because of their indifference.
Desires have become non-manifest; the net of views has been utterly destroyed.
Now that [desire] is rootless, from where could a dispute against you arise?
(9) Desires have become non-manifest; the net of views has been utterly destroyed. Now that it is rootless, from where could a dispute against you arise? (9)
When there is no basis, why would you engage in dispute over what is baseless?
Your afflictions have been extinguished and the net of false views destroyed; since you have no basis [for contention], from what basis could dispute arise for you?
O steadfast one, how could those like you, who have conquered and shine with victory, ever wish to dispute?
What dispute can there be between the thousand-rayed sun and the corpse-like darkness? O steadfast one, what need for you, who have attained sovereignty, to engage in such a quarrel?
What conflict can there be with darkness, which is like a corpse, even against the possessor of a thousand rays?
What could you, steadfast ones who appear like victors, dispute about? What conflict can there be between the thousand-rayed sun and dead darkness?
Dust goes against the wind; arguments do not take root in you, just as lashes of a whip do not stick in the sky. (11)
Just as one cannot strike the sky with a whip, you cannot be overcome by debate. Dust thrown against the wind falls back upon the thrower; likewise, words of dispute do not reach you.
The world has fallen into conceptual construction, while you have the sphere of activity that accords with reality as it is;
therefore, you do not agree with the many who have fallen into error.
12. The worlds have fallen into what is merely imagined; you, however, have the sphere of activity of things as they truly are.

Therefore, you do not share the same nature as the many who have fallen into error; for while they are attached to what is false, you are free from attachment. *vitathābhiniviṣṭānāṃ tvayānabhiniveśinā*
How could there be any commonality between you and those who are attached to the false?
(Verse 13) For example, just as iron and gold [are distinct], how could there be any conversation between you, who are free from attachment, and those who are perversely obsessed?

Between those who cling to falsehood and you, who are free from clinging [to false views], how could there be any commonality—just as, for example, between iron and gold? Fools, seeking you out as their protector and benefactor, fail to find you because of their ignorance; thus, through their own lack of understanding, they only bring ruin upon themselves. 14
The fools who challenge you— the Protector who desires their benefit and happiness, whom it is improper to challenge— through their ignorance, they bring about their own ruin by their own actions.
It would be better for me to cast myself upon a ground thickly strewn with garlands of blazing flames—
difficult to approach— than to ever encounter the Victors.
(15) I would rather throw myself into a mass of flickering, garlanded fire than ever meet the Jinas.

It would have been better for them to have cast themselves into a place filled with garlands of flames than to have dared to approach the Victors, who possess such radiant splendor that they are perilous to draw near.
Having challenged you in debate, they were summoned back...
Like those pierced by a firmly driven stake, you have been struck here by me with the challenge of debate;
having issued this challenge to you, you are unable to rise from your seat, as if bound by a tight tether. (1.6)
When the fangs of debate were broken by you,
O Sātyaki, in that assembly,
all those who propounded opposing views fell as if their horns had been struck down. (17)
Since you have broken the tusks of the disputant Satyaka in public,
the horns of all opposing adversaries have likewise been shattered.
Some adversaries falter, others sink down on all sides,
while yet others bow down upon encountering you.
(18) Some opponents, having met with you, submit themselves.
Some, having encountered you, retreat to a great distance; others approach your presence with dejection, while yet others are utterly defeated.
Others, however, have been drenched by you with the streams of the nectar of the True Dharma.
They honor the true Dharma, being perfected in its realization.
(19) Some, by the rain of the stream of nectar that you have let fall upon the sublime Dharma,
rely upon the true Dharma through their excellence in authentic practice.
Drenched by the streams of the nectar of your true Dharma, others follow that very truth and have fulfilled their religious goal.
Alas, O darkness! O you of wicked delusion! Alas, O Jālinī! Alas, O pride of vain form! Alas, O Lord, whose nature is compassion! 20
Alas, O Lord whose nature is compassion! Alas, wretched delusion and afflictions! Alas, proliferating craving! Alas, pride that brings about ruin! Oh, Lord!

Thrown into confusion by those three corrupting factors, this world is swept away from your teaching as if by a contrary current.
From these [three] roots, the two-fold paths of views and so forth spread out.
All secondary afflictions and defilements are individually obstacles to the path. By means of this basis, views, doubt,

On this basis, beginning with [wrong] views, doubts, and deviations, all secondary and primary afflictions spread forth, each acting as an obstacle on the [right] path.
One who has realized the flavor of Your Dharma does not cling to the doctrines of others, just as one who knows the song of the kalaviṅka bird does not take pleasure in the cries of crows. (23)

Just as one who has heard the song of the kalaviṅka bird finds no pleasure in the cawing of crows, so too, when one tastes the flavor of your Dharma, one will find no attachment to the words of others.

Even those who have entered the sphere of your speech by resorting to the pretext of the Dharma, they— who consume whatever comes their way— have attained the state of camel-honey. (24) Those who, having fabricated a sham of the Dharma, have entered into your teaching, [have become like camels eating honey].

But for those who were addicted to a counterfeit dharma and then entered the domain of your words— for those who consume whatever comes their way— it is like honey to a camel. [Your speech is] true, meaningful, consistent with its purpose, measured, and in accordance with the disposition [of the listener].
It possesses miracles, is exclusively of great power, and is imperishable. (25) It is true, easy to understand, and meaningful; it is endowed with intention and miracles;

It is true, it brings about understanding, it accords with the meaning, it is appropriate to the mental disposition [of the listeners], it is well-measured, accompanied by miraculous manifestations, entirely powerful, imperishable, substantial (*sāra*), possessing the essence of substance (*sārarasa*), possessed of synonyms (*paryāyavat*), possessed of skillful means (*upāyavat*), complete, unmixed, vigorous, and glorious. Possessing the supreme essence and the taste of essence, possessing various enumerations and skillful means, complete and unmixed, majestic and renowned.
Who would not listen to the words of one endowed with such qualities as these?

"Whether pleasant or unpleasant, that which is not beneficial is to be abandoned; in the opposite case, however, it is to be cultivated.
Since you speak with multiple perspectives regarding the pursuit of the desirable and the undesirable, how could those who speak from a single perspective ever follow your path? (29)
How could those who teach exclusively one-sidedly follow your path, which you have thus taught as being impartial regarding the cultivation of both the desirable and the undesirable?
That very purposefulness which you have taught regarding the performance of [these] practices is itself the sufficient boundary between your own doctrine and the doctrines of others.
(30) Whatever has been taught by you for the sake of those who engage in such conduct—
The very fact that your word and the words of others reach their respective conclusions,
and the state of being directed solely toward that which you have demonstrated through your deeds— this alone is sufficient to distinguish your teaching from the teachings of others.
It is not like the case of poison and nectar, nor like that of light and darkness.
Just as there is a vast difference between your teaching and the doctrines of others,
it is not like that of poison and nectar, nor is it like darkness and light. (3.1)
There is no such vast difference between poison and nectar, nor between light and darkness, as there is between your teaching and the teachings of others.
(32) There is no such vast difference between heaven and the lower realms, nor between ambrosia and putrid matter, as there is between your doctrine and the doctrines of others. (32)

The difference between your word and the words of others is as vast as that between the heavenly realms and the miserable states of existence; it is not merely like the difference between nectar and urine cast aside.
That [other system] consists of mere words as its essence, whereas this one possesses both words and their meanings;
by this, the difference between your doctrine and the doctrines of others has been explained.
(3.3) These two are mere words in their core, while this one is endowed with both words and their meanings.
By this, the distinction between your teaching and the words of others has been explained:

that [teaching] consists merely of objects of speech, whereas this [teaching] contains both words and meaning. Thus, the difference between your teaching and the teachings of other proponents is declared. (yad asti tava teṣāṃ ca vādināṃ sugatāntaram)

That very [distinction] between your doctrine and the doctrines of others, by virtue of being superior or inferior—O Sugata, what is the difference between you and those proponents? That itself constitutes the high and low status of your word and the words of others. || 34 ||

O Blessed One, that very same difference which exists between you and those teachers is also found through the disparity in level between your teaching and the teachings of others. Just as the difference between worldly existence and liberation is inconceivable, so too, O Great Hero, is the difference between your doctrine and the doctrines of others. (35)
Just as the distinction between cyclic existence and liberation is beyond comprehension, so too, O Hero, is the distinction between your teaching and the teachings of others.
O Victor, that which pertains to engagement and withdrawal, and that which pertains to affliction and purification— that alone is the difference between your teaching and the teachings of others.
(36) Whatever constitutes engagement and withdrawal, and whatever constitutes thorough affliction and complete purification— [that is the distinction].
O Hero, that very thing is the distinction between your word and the words of others.
Between arising and ceasing, and between defilement and purification—this alone, O Victor, is the difference between your teaching and the teachings of others.
Herein lies the absolute reality; everything else is merely of a deceptive nature.

What else could there be as the difference between your doctrine and the doctrines of others? (37) This alone is suchness; since it is solely of a deceptive nature, what other distinction could there be between your word and the speech of others?

On this page, there is complete conformity with reality, yet that [reality] is in its nature entirely deceptive. What other difference could there be between your teaching and the teachings of others? This one is exclusively beneficial, while that one is exclusively obstructive. What else, then, could be the disparity between your doctrine and the doctrines of others? (38)
This alone is exclusively wholesome, while that [other] is exclusively a source of obstacles; what difference, then, could there be between your teaching and the words of others?

In that regard, the purification of those who have been smeared and thoroughly anointed is prescribed here. This alone, O Lord, is the difference between your doctrine and the doctrines of others. (39) By this, they become purified through being smeared and thoroughly anointed.
"O Protector, this alone is the distinction between your word and the words of others:
that which is impure and defiled elsewhere receives purification here. This indeed, O Lord, is the difference between your teaching and the teachings of others!
All else is mere idle chatter; this alone is well-spoken."

By him, the relative strength and weakness of your own doctrine and the doctrines of others has been upheld. It is not that this [other] is well-spoken; rather, for that reason, the certainty regarding the authority of your word and the words of others has been established.

All false chatter consists of those [other teachings]; this alone is the one correct utterance. By it is carried the balance of power between your teaching and the teachings of others. In both worldly involvement and withdrawal, that which is the nature of this world—
whom all the diverse worlds, together with their gods, do not transcend.
What is the nature of this world in its engagement and withdrawal, and from what does the entire world, including the gods, never deviate?

That which is the basis of this world in its arising and passing away, which no ordinary person together with the gods is able to transcend— that *saddharmasāvitrī* consisting of twelve lines in forward and reverse order has been fully revealed by you, O Sun of the True Dharma.
"In accordance with and contrary to the system, the two syllables of the twelve phrases— these you have revealed as the *sāvitrī* of the True Dharma, O Sāvitrī of the True Dharma, worthy of worship."
That same *triṣṭubh* [meter], due to the deficiency of its members, is transformed fourfold in each respective member within a single spontaneously born existence. (3) That very [meter],
in one spontaneously born existence, due to the incompleteness of its members...
Just as it was, by repeating each limb four times, there are three [verses] of offering;
thus, this very *triṣṭubh*—due to the absence of one limb in each spontaneously appearing form—is individually transformed limb by limb into a fourfold [structure].
Furthermore, through the completeness of its limbs, that same [verse] becomes a *jagatī* with twelve syllables.

By means of the feet and the method of truth, it is transformed as before. From the complete set of limbs, by means of the twelve syllables and phrases, if one applies the sequence of truth as previously described, it constitutes a supreme progression.
Furthermore, this very [brahman], by virtue of the completeness of its constituent parts, is transformed—just as before—in the correct manner into a *jagatī* consisting of twelve-syllable verses.
"O Brahman, those brahmins who worship this three-fold *brahman* according to the rule, they become one with *brahman* under your teaching. (5)
O Brahmā, those brāhmaṇas who properly honor this threefold purifying Brahma in your teaching become one with Brahmā; they are the Brahmās of your doctrine.

The state of a brahmin, the brahmins themselves, the very fruit of being a brahmin, and the purpose of the brahmin state, O Subrahman—none of these exist apart from your teaching. (6) The way of the Brahmin, the Brahmin himself, the fruit of the Brahmin way, and the goal of the Brahmin—all these [are found] nowhere else than in your instruction. (6)
O Supreme Brahmā, apart from your teaching, there exists nowhere else a true brahmin, nor indeed anything called brahminhood, nor the fear of brahminhood, nor the benefit of brahminhood.
O Excellent Brahmā, other than brahminhood, no one at all is found who is truly a brahmin.
And this direct path does not exist anywhere else; Without the way of Brahmā, no one can become a brāhmaṇa. This straight path, moreover, does not belong to anyone else.

There is no true brahmin without the state of being a brahmin, nor is this straight path found anywhere else: "The brahmins know one who is perfected in knowledge and conduct as a brahmin; that knowledge and that conduct are not found elsewhere than in your teaching. (8)
The Brahmins explain that one who is endowed with knowledge and conduct is a true *brāhmaṇa*. Yet such knowledge and such conduct do not exist elsewhere than in your teaching.
For those sciences belong to those in training and those beyond training, and they bring about that conduct;
indeed, for this one who abides in the Dharma, no other name is found. Those sciences belong to those in training and those beyond training; they are what bring about that conduct.
Furthermore, even the name of that path of Dharma does not exist elsewhere. For by entering it, all castes become twice-born; yet even the name of this path of Dharma does not exist anywhere else.
By you, that door to immortality, which had long been closed, has been opened.
By means of that which you have practiced, you have opened the door to immortality— which had been shut for a long time— that brings all castes to the status of Brahmins.

That gate to immortality, long closed, through which all castes become twice-born upon entering—this you have opened. What kind of Brahmin could there be who is seized by false views and doubt? These knots are not severed anywhere else except through your teaching. (11)
How could one who is consumed by wrong views and doubt become a brahmin? Apart from your system, these knots cannot be severed by any other.
"Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his heart and his mouth"—
this worldly proverb has now found its fulfillment in you. (12) "O Brahmin, you are the son of Brahmā, born from his heart and his mouth."
"That which is renowned in the world has become fruitful for you:

'The Brāhmaṇas are the sons of Brahmā, legitimate, born from his mouth'—this widespread common view has found its fulfillment in you. You are Brahmā; the path to Brahmā is yours; in you, O bull among Brāhmaṇas, is that [path] realized."
You are the leader and the initiator; you are the officiant and the domestic priest.
You are Brahmā, and you possess the path of Brahmā; you are the preeminent bull among brahmins, as well as the guide and the teacher.
You are the seasonal sacrificer and the presiding priest.

You are Brahmā; in you exists the path belonging to Brahmā. You are the most excellent among brahmins, the leader (*praṇetṛ*), and the guide (*upanetṛ*); you are the sacrificial priest (*hotṛ*) and the domestic chaplain (*purohita*).
No one made impure by you becomes a non-brahmin, nor does a brahmin fall from his status as a brahmin simply because he has been initiated (*upanīta*). 14
No brahmin purified by you will become impure, nor will a brahmin initiated by you fall away from the way of Brahmā.
The three truths of the Brahmins, the threefold characteristics of the Brahmins,
the three lineages of the Brahmins, and the three eminent ancestors of the Brahmins.

There are not the three supreme Brahmas, nor is there even a Brahmin lineage; for nowhere does the proper conduct of a Brahmin exist, nor is there the Brahmin path anywhere.

O Brahmin, there are no qualities of a brahmin other than your teaching. Apart from your instruction, there is no way to become a brahmin; there is neither the sacrifice to Brahmā nor the path to Brahmā.

For there is no right conduct of a brāhmaṇa, nowhere the brāhmaṇa path, nor the factors by which one becomes a brāhmaṇa, outside of your teaching. Whatever is well-spoken in the world, all that comes from your instruction; this faultless eloquence is indeed unique to the Sugata. (17)
Whatever well-spoken words exist in the world, all arise from your teaching; this faultless eloquence is unique to the Sugata alone.
But those others who are seen to possess faultless verbal conduct,
O Knower of All Dharmas, they all subsist on the remnants of your well-spoken words.
(18) Those others besides you who are seen to have faultless speech—

O Brahmin, you are the one who has spoken well; all those others besides you who are observed to possess flawless conduct of speech are, O Knower of All Dharmas, merely consumers of the remnants of what you have rightly spoken.
Whatever is well-spoken among outsiders is seen to be like the accidental letter carved by a wood-boring insect.

Therefore, that which is of a different nature [from this work], like gold upon iron, or like letters gnawed by insects— whatever well-spoken words exist here other than these— are not appropriate for it, just as gold is not appropriate for iron. (19)
Whatever is found among those outside [this teaching] regarding well-spoken words—resembling, as it were, a letter carved by a woodworm—is of such a dissimilar nature there, like gold amidst iron.
Who would have faith in that which is contradicted from beginning to end, like sandalwood of the *gośīrṣa* variety placed upon castor-oil plants? (20)

Who would place their trust in that [well-spoken word] within that other teaching, where it is contradicted from beginning to end, like planting the finest sandalwood, *gośīrṣa*, in a thicket of castor-oil plants?
He who would believe that mango fruits, ripe and pale, could grow upon *nimba* trees— that person has faith in the "well-spoken words" (subhāṣita) only regarding external things.
(21) Whoever [would believe] that mango fruits, ripe and attached, [could grow] on *nimba* trees...

One who, seeing mango fruits turned yellow by ripeness on nimba trees, thinks, "Therefore they have originated from those [mango trees]," might as well believe that there are well-spoken words among those outside this teaching.
For in this world, including the gods, there are no jewels of well-spoken words [other than these].
Just as sandalwood originates from Malaya, there is no source for the jewel of well-spoken teachings other than you in this world, including the gods.
(22) Just as sandalwood [originates] from Malaya, there is no source for the jewel of well-spoken teachings in this world, including the gods, other than you. (22)
For the jewels of the well-spoken [words] in this world together with its gods, there is no other source than you, just as for sandalwood there is no source other than the Malaya mountains.

With eyes that turn to the right, single-lashed, upturned, soft and stainless, glossy, with the luster of dense sapphire, unattached and straight-aimed— 21.
O Sugata, your body is like the heart of a golden lotus;
each hair curls to the right, soft, stainless, and grows upward.

By means of [the rays] directed to the right, growing individually, upward-turned, soft, stainless, oily, possessing the dull luster of sapphires, unconfined, and straight—[which are] like the interior of a *surā* lotus—the limbs of you, the Sugata, [are compared] with those born from the limbs of the Sugata.
It shines as if inlaid with fine jeweled earrings; smooth, unblemished, and undisturbed, it appears as if adorned with minute gems, encircled by blue jewels like the hue of Indra-nīla.
By these body hairs, your body—which resembles the calyx of a divine lotus, O Sugata—shines like it were shimmering with fine jeweled bracelets.
That mark of the unique, singular hair (*nāgāveṇika-lakṣaṇa*) belonging to you, the Naga among men, is utterly undefiled by external or internal impurities. (23)
O elephant among men, that which is your own elephantine mark— untainted by any external or internal impurity— is utterly stainless.

O one of beautiful limbs, that limb of yours which is joined [with an ornament] is pure and excellent; O one of beautiful limbs, that limb of yours which resembles an ornament is well-composed. (24) Whatever limb of yours is like an ornament, that beautiful limb is excellent.
Like a seamless ornament cast from pure gold, it stands like a surrounding rim; O Well-Shaped One, this member of yours is fitting,
possessing the beauty of the space between the thighs of the foremost of all noble steeds.
Having surpassed the beautiful physical forms of all the preeminent thoroughbred horses, he remained there, eclipsing their auspicious masculine marks with his own exquisite beauty. (25)

Because of the excellence of the configuration of his own body, which surpasses the beauty of the private parts of all those who stand at the head of the noble lineage, you are indeed naked, O Protector, yet for you it is as if you were not naked. (26)
O Protector, because you dwell in pure conduct and because your form is exceedingly beautiful, that which is indeed shameful for others is not shameful in you.
Out of compassion for those who are in doubt, you have revealed [the truth] through a mere fraction of another sign,
like the orb of the moon appearing through a gap in the clouds.
(27) Out of compassion for those who are in doubt, you have [revealed it] by way of another sign...

Having shaken the mountain of shame and dread, you have repeatedly shown even those who are wavering— just as the form of the moon appears through a rift in the clouds— as a mere small portion within the signs of your compassion.
That which was made an object of the eye’s cognition through great compassion—
having caused the mountain of shame and modesty to tremble as if it were unshakable—
that which was made an object of the eye’s cognition by means of great compassion.
O Unshakable One, you who have made the mountain of conscience and shame an object for the eye through your great compassion—
[that which was] slightly [touched by] the whorls of filaments of the lotuses of the Mandākinī,
such was the beauty of the hair-whorls on your noble body, O Teacher. (29)
The beauty of the whorls of filaments of slightly opened *mandākinī* lotuses cannot disturb the loveliness of the whorl of hair on your noble limb, O Protector!
If there were a whorl situated upon the full moon of Lakṣmīvat,
it would not even reach the level of comparison for his excellent head.
(30) Even if there were a whorl situated upon the glorious full moon, [it could not compare].
Nevertheless,
even if a *ūrṇā* were to exist upon the auspicious full moon, it would not suffice as a basis for comparison with your preeminent limb.
For what indeed could compare to that which is so beautiful, fashioned from noble deeds of a hundred merits?
Will another volition projected by that [previous one] follow upon its path?
Upon the beautiful road manifested by karma consisting of hundreds of vast merits, will it be pursued again by a volition other than that? (31)
But what could possibly equal that which is so beautiful because it was fashioned from karma rich with a hundredfold merit, once released from a different state of mind?
Even though well-concealed by the restraint of its own sheath and garments, it seems to attain visibility through the excellence of its remaining characteristics. (32)
Although well-concealed by its own sheath, its clothing, and self-restraint, it becomes as if clearly manifest through the perfection of its other marks.
I honor that excellent limb of yours, O you who possess excellent limbs, bowing my head with a mind full of serene faith and with words as well.
(33) I honor that supreme limb of yours, O you who possess excellent limbs, bowing my head with a mind full of serene faith and with words as well.

With my head bowed and a mind of profound faith, I shall worship with speech as well this supreme limb, you who possess the most excellent limbs and whose sight is never satiating.
*Agrye prasādanīyānām asecanakadarśane* (To you, the foremost among those worthy of inspiration, whose appearance is never enough to behold).
If there is resentment toward you— the supreme among those to whom one should pay homage, whom one can never tire of beholding— then fie upon that blind and most base darkness!
Before the foremost of the delightful, whom one can never behold enough—if you harbor aversion toward him, then alas for that blind and deepest darkness!

Just as the inclinations of sentient beings abide according to their respective realms,
so too does my own intention remain abundant within this vast [realm].
Since the inclinations of sentient beings abide according to their respective elements,
for the time being, my own thought is that [the teaching] should be extensive upon the broad tongue.
The inclinations of sentient beings are fixed according to their respective dispositions; accordingly, I have the greatest interest in the Great [Tongue].
Who would not honor with head, mind, and speech this abundant one, who is the mother of this entire teaching and the source of all jewels? 2.
Who would not worship with head, mind,
and voice the Great One,
whose tongue is vast, who is the Mother of this entire Word of the Buddha and the progenitress of jewels?
O Lord, this abundant eloquence of yours shines forth for me as the most unsurpassed among all unsurpassed deeds.
This broad tongue within your mouth appears to me as the unsurpassed pinnacle of all your supreme faculties, O Lord.
Having attained the office of Dharma, your teaching is renowned throughout the world.
For she stands at the head of all the marks, like a queen at the front of a procession.
Proclaiming the teaching to those who go before, she abides as the foremost among all the marks, like a king, for the sake of performing the enlightened activity of the Dharma.
For, having been appointed to the office of the Dharma, she whose commands are proclaimed throughout the world stands, as it were, like a queen at the head of all the marks.
That which was brought forth from her mouth for the sake of dispelling the doubts of others,
like a streak of clouds at the autumnal twilight, eclipses the moon of her face.
To dispel the doubts of others, she extends [her tongue] from her mouth; like a mass of autumn clouds at twilight, it veils the moon of her face.

What could be more wonderful than this: that she, though being so vast and beautiful, lies without constraint within the mouth crowded with teeth? (6) Thus, she who is so expansive and lovely rests within the interior of the face, which is filled with teeth.

What could be more marvelous than this: that although it is so broad and beautiful, it lies without constraint within a mouth constricted by teeth? This lack of deficiency in her auspiciousness, her delicacy, and her softness— anūnam etat kalyāṇyāḥ saukumāryamṛdutvayoḥ |
The power of this [teaching] will be immeasurable in its majesty;
it is the power of that very one who is certainly endowed with immeasurable, excellent, and exceedingly gentle and pleasant qualities.
This must be entirely the power of the subtlety and delicacy of those Exalted Ones who possess immeasurable might:
"Possessing the brilliance of molten Jāmbūnada gold and the luster of glowing copper, you create a garland of lightning within your cloud-thundering mouth. (8)

When your mouth resounds with the roar of thunder, it creates a flash of lightning like a garland of flickering light, resembling molten gold from the Jambu River and the brilliance of refined copper.
Having attained what is like the sovereignty of supreme kingship through the excellence of his training, the Goddess of Eloquence moves at will within his mouth, sporting in various places.
(9) Having acquired the sovereign power of excellent training, she dwells freely within his mouth, delighting in various locations. (9)
Having attained mastery over the perfection of training and artistic skill, she moves at will within your mouth, like one who sports by shifting between various positions.
She releases these faultless flowers of speech.
Having smelled whose fragrance you are celebrated as the "Flower-Speaker," those very flowers of faultless speech are being strewn here by this [person].
This [tongue] emits those faultless flowers of speech, the fragrance of which you smell and for which you are praised as the "Flower-Speaker.
For this very reason, it flows forth that honey which is exceedingly sweet; because of its exquisite flavor, O Jina, you are renowned as the "Honey-Speaker. (11)
For this very reason, from you, O Victor, flows this most sweet honey; because of its exquisite fragrance, you, O Conqueror, are renowned as "He Who Speaks Honey" (Madhuvādin).
It is precisely here that this instruction and guidance is bound up;
by its power, those like you are made illustrious as givers of the nectar of immortality.
(12) By whose power those like you are renowned as bestowers of the nectar of immortality.

The instruction and guidance depend upon this very [text], by whose power those like you are empowered as givers of nectar. This has been accomplished by that virtuous woman, who disregarded her own weariness.
By this merit, may he turn the wheel of Dharma in the world including the gods— [he] who, by that [turning],
does not perceive his own exhaustion. (13)
By her this was accomplished—by that Exalted One who disregarded her own exhaustion, through whom the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion in the world together with its gods.
(14) Great is her majesty, by which this world is illuminated, strewn with hundreds of well-spoken words as if filled with a heap of jewels. (14)
That by which this world is illuminated, filled with hundreds of well-spoken words as if strewn with heaps of jewels— that is their power.
The Noble One, who ordains all phenomena, speaks with logic and eloquence; like the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree, she bestows the fruits of various jewels.
(15) She is the Noble One who proclaims the lineage and the conduct, speaking of all phenomena.
Like a branch of the wish-fulfilling tree, she bestows the fruit of various jewels.
As the distributor of all dharmas, one who speaks both coherently and freely, the Noble One is like a tendril of the wish-fulfilling tree that grants various precious fruits as its rewards.

Who in this world, other than Prabhūtā, could bear the burden of inspired eloquence that is embraced by omniscience? (16)
In this world,
who could bear the burden of eloquence— the eloquence of the specific perfect knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) belonging to one endowed with omniscience— were it not for a broad tongue?

Who in the world, other than the Great [Tongue], could lift up the weight of the brilliance that resides within the specialized knowledge of brilliance, which is enveloped by omniscience? For whatever teachings you two present together to her, she, untiring, strings them together like flowers. (17)
Whatever various dharmas you have taught with intention to them, you have strung them together like a garland of flowers without weariness.
Who could know your true omniscience, who your true great compassion,
or who your other existing virtues, if this [scripture] were not to reveal them?
(18) If this were not revealed by you, who would recognize your omniscience?

Who would know that you truly possess great compassion? Who would know that you truly possess the other qualities? For those like you are not made manifest without teaching. na hi santaḥ prakāśyante tvādṛśā deśanām ṛte |
And the teaching rests upon the *Prabhūta* [Sūtra], just as success rests upon logic.
If the teachings did not exist, scholars such as you would not appear; and the teaching, moreover, relies upon the broad tongue, just as the attainment of realization relies upon the scriptures. (19)
No one like you is made manifest, even if they truly exist, except through instruction; and instruction depends upon the Great Tongue (*mahājihvā*), just as a proof depends upon logical inference.
It speaks various kinds of teachings and consumes various kinds of flavors;
yet, unlike the sky which is not stained by mud, it is not defiled by attachment to flavors. (20)
Though he proclaims various teachings and tastes various flavors, he is not defiled by attachment to taste, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.

Conducive to silence yet untiring even in speaking, she alone partakes equally in both dharmas, whether they be similar or dissimilar. (21) She conforms to remaining silent, and she is never weary of speaking.
She is inclined toward silence, yet she never tires of teaching; thus, she alone possesses a share in both these seemingly contradictory qualities.
Excellent through being well-bred, she flows evenly everywhere.
(22) She does not feel weary when remaining silent, nor does she feel fatigue when teaching;
she is virtuous through her omniscience and enters into equanimity toward all.
She is not bored when remaining silent, nor does she grow weary while teaching; due to her noble lineage, the Exalted One moves with equal composure everywhere.
Oh, what a range of conduct! Oh, what single-minded dedication to the right method!
She is capable of saying everything, yet she speaks only of the Dharma. (23)
Thus, though she is capable of speaking all things, she utters only the Dharma; her devotion to conduct is marvelous, and her inclination toward reason is also marvelous.

She is eternally perfumed by material merit, by that consisting of the proclamation of the Dharma, and by the two unsurpassed fragrances of the Buddha. (24) By means of the merit derived from the elements and by the nature of the teaching of the Dharma, she is eternally perfumed by the two unsurpassed fragrances of the Buddha. (24)
It is constantly perfumed by two unsurpassed, Buddha-like fragrances: that which arises from the merits of the elements and that which originates from the proclamation of the Dharma;
and by its pure, visible splendor, which consists of glorious renown.
Renowned in all directions through both types of radiance and through her two [pure] colors; by virtue of the purity of the range of her eyes and the nature of her merit and fame.

By the purity of the domain of her vision and by the essence of her merit and renown.
She is renowned in every direction through two kinds of fame:
that which is visible to the eye and that which consists of the renown of her merit. Blessed are those eyes, and blessed are those people who possess them.
Those by whom she, whose every limb is faultless, was seen as she emerged from his mouth—
they alone possess true vision; and those eyes are truly blessed.

Blessed are those eyes, and truly possessed of eyes are those people who have beheld with their own mouths this [speech] which is flawless in every limb. But they are most fortunate indeed, by whom her eloquence in speech has been drunk directly with the hollowed palms of their ears, like liquid nectar. (27)
But those wise ones are most fortunate who have directly drunk his melodious speech with ears hollowed like the palms of hands in the gesture of salutation, as if it were a stream of nectar.
It seems to adorn the phonemes, it seems to embellish the earth with phonemes;
it makes your face appear even more worthy of being accepted when spoken. (28) As if adorning the sounds, as if embellishing the earth with sounds...

When you deliver your teaching, your face appears as if it were being kept deeply concealed; yet it adorns the sounds, and with those sounds it adorns your speech; when addressed, it leads your mouth to an even greater loveliness.
O Sage, for you whose moon-like face has become an ornament for the world—

(29) By her own quality of beauty, this [face] of yours, O Sage, which is already an ornament to the world, has become an even more sublime ornament. (29)
O Sage, for this moon of your face, which has become the ornament of the world, she has become as it were an even greater ornament due to the quality of her own beauty;
because of her color, form, eloquence, delicacy, and majesty, I do not see any material object anywhere that possesses a form equal to hers. (30)
In terms of color, shape, melodious resonance, extreme softness, and power, I have not seen any material object among embodied beings that resembles the broad tongue [of the Great One].
If that goddess Sarasvatī exists as some embodied being,
she will be this one of perfectly faultless limbs, for she is abundant [in merit].
(31) If that goddess Sarasvatī exists as some embodied being...
"This [tongue] of yours,
which is faultless in all its parts and broad— this must surely be the goddess Sarasvatī herself! All sounds, whether divine or human, become utterly tasteless.
When the vast tongue has begun to strike the drum of Dharma,
all the sounds of gods and humans will become devoid of flavor.
All celestial and human sounds become tasteless as soon as the Great [Tongue] has begun to beat the drum of the Dharma.
You are the speaker, this is the instrument, and this is the unsurpassed speech;
this threefold medicine dispels the poison of all afflictions. (33)
O Teacher, you, this tongue of yours, and this unsurpassed speech— these three constitute the supreme medicine that destroys the poison of all afflictions.

I do not perceive the ultimate limit of that karma which consists in my improper conduct toward you, who are most worthy of veneration;

Whatever wrong engagement there may be toward you,
who have reached the culmination of the perfect practice— that action, too, reaches no end in its culmination of ruin.

Thus, I perceive no limit to the deterioration of that karma consisting of your misconduct toward me, you who have reached the culmination of right conduct. Fie upon that ignoble impermanence, which has struck even you, who are endowed with power in every respect! (6)
Alas for this vulgar impermanence, which knows no bounds, by which even you— who possess power in every respect— have been struck down!
Oh, the wretchedness of cyclic existence! Oh, the peace of nirvāṇa!

For even one such as you, a self-controlled master whose very nature is compassion, has entered therein. Oh, how miserable is the nature of saṃsāra! Oh, how peaceful is nirvāṇa! That even a master like you, whose essence is compassion, has gone there.

The fear of the future has not been declared; the guiding principle has not been set in motion.
He spoke of the fears of the future and explained the way of the Dharma;
he caused the fourfold assembly to attain fearlessness.
Surely the future danger was foretold; surely the leadership was provided; surely fearlessness was granted to the four assemblies.
Yet Ma(hākāśyapa), Ānanda, and the others, though they had attained wisdom, were not appointed for the protection of this auspicious [teaching]. (9)
Although wise men such as Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda have been appointed for the sake of guarding this excellent path, they have indeed been purified in their intellect.
When you, the stainless single eye of the world,
have closed [your eyes], this world, even though the light of truth exists, is as if shrouded in darkness. (10) When you, the sole stainless eye of the world, have closed [your eyes]...
Although there was light, this world was as if shrouded in darkness;
yet, O Sugata, you have brought about the state of the Sugatas.
These very ones are your true sons—the learners and those beyond learning, your own legitimate offspring.
O Sugata, although these words of yours, the Sugata, exist, and these excellent sons of yours—the learners and those beyond learning—also exist; || 11 ||

Indeed, there is this teaching of the Well-Gone One (*sugata*), and likewise these true sons— both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)— who are your own sons; yet, O Lord of the World, without you, the universe has passed into another state,
like a sky whose limbs are the bright planets and stars, yet empty of the moon.
If you, the protector of beings, do not remain, this world will be utterly ruined and no longer exist, like the sky— marked by bright planets and stars— when it is empty of the moon.

[If you were not present], this [scripture]— its excellence and vitality fading away, its flaws exposed by the wounds inflicted by other systems as if by the end of an eon— would be like the splendor of a lake whose nāgas have departed.
(13) If you were not present, this word of the Buddha would be like the glory of a lake from which the nāgas have fled.
Like a long-lasting vessel that perishes,
this teaching’s excellence has vanished through its separation from the essential core, as wounds and vulnerabilities have arisen due to other rules and other doctrines.
Apart from you, the prosperity of this scripture has come to an end.
Like the fleeting splendor of a lake whose serpents have been snatched away;
since you have extracted both the thorn and the wound through other methods and other systems, even the majesty of the body has faded away. (14) Do not despise even minor qualities;
for by means of other rituals and other traditions, both the thorn and the wound have been extracted, and thus the vigor of the body has vanished. (14)

Without you, it has undergone change like the swiftly vanishing beauty of a lake deprived of its serpent deity. Who would not have fear of existences that are like flaming swords, when one considers the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas who possess mastery? (15)
When one contemplates the *parinirvāṇa* of the Buddhas who wield sovereign power, who would not feel fear toward existences that resemble flaming swords?
